synthesis.headline: A north-driven regime holds into a fourth day: an Arctic/Hudson Bay trough anchors Canada, a cold front clears the East, and the heat ridge contracts toward the Southwest
synthesis.narrative:
The continent's initiative stays in the north, as it has for several days. On the Canadian analysis a sprawling, multi-center area of low pressure dominates the interior from the western Prairies through the Great Lakes and into the Northeast, with a cool 1034 hPa high on its western flank and a deep 988 hPa cyclone offshore east of the Maritimes carrying the tightest Canadian gradient. This is the same regime Tlaloc has tracked since midweek, now in roughly its fourth day. Downstream over the US, the day's active feature is a cold front tied to a shortwave trough over the Upper Midwest and a modest 1008 mb low, sweeping east through the Great Lakes and Ohio Valley — where isobars compress most sharply. A separate, weaker boundary drapes from a 1008-1009 mb low near the Texas-Oklahoma border into the Gulf, ahead of deep moisture (upper-70s dewpoints) fed by the 1017 mb Gulf Coast high. Across the interior West the three modest anticyclones (1023 mb northern Plains, 1019 mb Colorado, 1016 mb Desert Southwest) leave a slack gradient and suppressed convergence.

Today's severe threat is limited and marginal. SPC carries a Marginal Risk from the Ohio Valley into the Northeast and across the central and northern High Plains: along the eastern front, 35-45 kt deep-layer shear supports a few initial supercells that transition to clusters and bowing segments with an isolated damaging-wind risk before weakening overnight, and the front exits into the Atlantic by tomorrow. Out west, isolated storms fire ahead of a closed upper low moving into the northern Rockies, with elevated convection increasing into Monday. The more persistent hazard is hydrologic: WPC flags daily thunderstorm rounds and a flash-flood concern across the Heartland under the consolidating Northwest system, plus active North American Monsoon convection with excessive-rainfall risk over the Four Corners and southern Rockies. Beneath the residual southern ridge, record heat threatens the Southern Plains and Mid-Mississippi Valley into the work week. In Mexico, a compact, well-organized cyclonic vortex with a deep-convective core sits over southern Mexico near the Gulf of Tehuantepec — a feature worth watching in an already busy East Pacific.

The COD 500 mb analysis is unavailable today, so the upper-level read leans on the Air Mass RGB and the CPC height fields. The imagery is internally consistent with the surface story: a filamentary, cyclonically curling dry streamer around the Upper Midwest shortwave has the geometry of a genuine high-PV intrusion on the equatorward-cyclonic flank of the trough driving the eastern front, while the broad red-orange over the southern US and northern Mexico is warm-season subsidence beneath the summer ridge, not a stratospheric signature — its spatial extent argues against that read. A sharp airmass boundary arcs across the south-central and southeastern US, marking the likely jet corridor that separates tropical green air to the south from the drier north.

On the week's central question — does the interior ridge rebuild once this front clears — the ensemble pair says no, but with a geographic twist. The 6-10 day chart (Sep 18-22) shows a deep Arctic cutoff over the Canadian Archipelago with a downstream trough dug into central Canada, and a modest western ridge (+5 to +10 dam) over the Southwest, western Plains, and western Canada, with the zero-anomaly line through the central CONUS. By 8-14 days (Sep 20-26) the Arctic trough persists, positively tilted toward Hudson Bay, while the ridge core retreats westward and southward toward the central and southern Rockies and the anomalies over western Canada weaken further. So rather than rebuilding inland, the ridge contracts toward the Southwest while the north stays under Arctic influence — the classic retreat-not-collapse signature, and continuity with the withdrawal Tlaloc has flagged all week. The one honest nuance: today's 6-10 shows a touch more onshore ridge presence than yesterday's outlook implied, but it still shrinks by the longer lead rather than amplifying. The two-lobed warm temperature outlook (Northwest and Southeast cores, a central-interior minimum) is geometrically consistent with this ridge-trough-ridge, meridional regime holding rather than flattening.
synthesis.climate_context: ENSO is in a warm phase: after last winter's weak La Niña faded (NDJ ONI near -0.60), the index has warmed through neutral and into El Niño, with anomalies running toward roughly +1.8 by late summer 2026. The tropics fit that state cleanly. At what is climatologically the peak of the Atlantic season, the basin is nearly shut down — only a central subtropical Atlantic trough with a low-end (20 percent) chance of gradual development by mid-to-late week — while the East Pacific is busy, with Tropical Storm Norbert active and a low southwest of Baja California carrying an 80 percent chance of becoming a depression within 48 hours. That basin split, plus the disorganized Caribbean and Central American convection, is a textbook El Niño signature. Seasonally, late-summer severe weather is behaving in its expected northern-tier, ridge-periphery and frontal mode rather than as deep-Plains outbreaks, and the North American Monsoon remains active over the Southwest and interior Mexico. Teleconnections are a weak-season cross-check only: a modestly negative PNA is consistent with western ridging and eastern troughing, and a recently negative NAO (7-day mean near -1.01) with a more retarded, cut-off-prone downstream Atlantic flow — but today's story rests on the height and PV fields, not the indices.
synthesis.regional_notes: SPC has no active mesoscale discussions and is monitoring no organized convective threat at this hour. The sharpest sub-synoptic items are hydrologic: a flash-flood-sensitive corridor across the Heartland under repeated daily thunderstorm rounds, and excessive-rainfall potential over the Four Corners and southern Rockies in the active monsoon airmass. Record-challenging heat is likely over the Southern Plains and Mid-Mississippi Valley into the work week beneath the residual southern ridge. In Canada, the 988 hPa cyclone offshore east of the Maritimes holds the strongest winds on its eastern flank. Over Mexico, watch the compact, deep-convective vortex near the Gulf of Tehuantepec.

sources.title: Surface Analysis
sources.summary:
The chart is valid 0900Z Sunday 13 September 2026. The dominant features are a pair of well-separated anticyclones: a 1023 mb high centered over the northern Plains and a 1019 mb high over the central Rockies/Colorado area, with a third 1016 mb high over the Desert Southwest. These are not exceptional values but together they produce a broad, slack gradient across the interior West, consistent with suppressed surface convergence there. A more consequential high of 1017 mb sits over the Gulf Coast region, and isobar spacing there is moderate, supporting a southerly moisture feed — dewpoints in the upper 70s F are visible across the Gulf states, pointing to a deep moist airmass ahead of the frontal zone.

The main frontal boundary runs from a low near the Texas-Oklahoma border (central pressure around 1008-1009 mb, a modest system) eastward as a warm front and then southward as a cold front through the lower Mississippi Valley into the Gulf, where it is labeled as a stationary or outflow boundary segment. A separate cold front is trailing southward from a low in the upper Midwest (near 1008 mb), with the frontal zone extending through the Great Lakes into the Ohio Valley. The tightest pressure gradient on the chart is along and ahead of this Midwest cold front, where isobars compress noticeably from the western Great Lakes southward toward the Tennessee Valley, concentrating both lift and low-level shear in that corridor.

The combination of the 1008 mb Midwest low, the trailing cold front, and the rich Gulf moisture with dewpoints in the mid-to-upper 70s over Louisiana, Mississippi, and Alabama is where the chart focuses the greatest potential for organized lift and moisture convergence; the surface boundary over the lower Mississippi Valley is the key axis.

sources.title: Canadian Surface Analysis
sources.summary: This CMC surface analysis valid 0000Z Sunday 13 September 2026 shows a sprawling area of low pressure dominating the Canadian interior, with multiple centers threading from the western Prairies through the Great Lakes region and into the northeastern corner of the continent. A well-defined high of 1034 hPa sits over what appears to be the northern Great Plains or southern Canadian Prairies, with tightly packed isobars on its eastern flank implying a strong pressure gradient and implied northerly to northwesterly flow across that corridor. A series of frontal boundaries, including what appear to be cold and warm front segments, extend southward from lows near the Great Lakes area into the central and eastern United States, connecting the Canadian pattern to active systems well south of the border. Along the eastern Canadian seaboard, a low near 988 hPa sits offshore with an associated frontal tail sweeping across Atlantic Canada, while a high of 1026 hPa occupies what appears to be the far upper right of the frame consistent with high pressure over Greenland or the North Atlantic. The upper portion of the chart over the Arctic Archipelago shows broadly spaced isobars with modest lows, unremarkable for that region in this season.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB (GOES-19)
sources.summary: This GOES-19 Air Mass RGB from 13 September 2026 at 1321Z shows a broad swath of green (tropical moist air) dominating the Gulf Coast states and much of the central and eastern CONUS, consistent with an active warm-season moisture regime. A prominent cyclonic system with a compact, bright white deep-convective core is visible over southern Mexico near the Gulf of Tehuantepec region, with curved banding suggesting a well-organized tropical or subtropical vortex. A sharp airmass boundary arcs across the south-central and southeastern US, separating the tropical green air to the south from a more mixed region to the north, and this boundary marks the likely jet corridor at that latitude. Across the northern tier from the central Plains through the Great Lakes and into the Northeast, a red-orange dry signature with a thin, elongated streamer curling cyclonically around what appears to be a shortwave trough over the Upper Midwest suggests a genuine dry intrusion on the equatorward-cyclonic flank of that feature, appropriate for high-PV attribution given its position and geometry. Scattered white deep-convective cells are embedded along and ahead of this boundary from the Ohio Valley into the Mid-Atlantic, with additional convection visible over Cuba and the western Caribbean.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB Full Disk (GOES-19)
sources.summary: The most prominent airmass boundary visible on this image runs across southern Canada and curves into the North Atlantic, marked by the sharp transition from the deep blue-purple tones (cold, dry upper troposphere) in the high latitudes to the green tropical airmass dominating the tropics and subtropics. A broad swath of red-orange color covers much of the subtropical eastern Pacific and extends across the southern United States and northern Mexico, consistent with dry, subsident upper-tropospheric air under a summer ridge rather than a stratospheric intrusion. In the deep tropics, scattered clusters of bright white convective tops are visible over Central America, the southern Gulf of Mexico, and the western Caribbean, with additional cells over equatorial South America near the Colombian and Venezuelan coasts. A tightly curved cyclonic vortex is clearly visible in the southern South Atlantic near the bottom-left of the disk, with the characteristic blue-purple airmass wrapping around it and an implied dry intrusion spiraling into the circulation on its poleward flank — this compact geometry does support a high-PV reading for that Southern Hemisphere feature. The North Atlantic basin shows a broad shield of mid- and high-level cloud curving from the Canadian Maritimes toward western Europe, consistent with an active baroclinic zone along the northern rim of the image.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day Temperature Outlook
sources.summary:
The dominant signal on this chart is a broad above-normal temperature signal covering virtually the entire contiguous United States, with the highest probabilities concentrated in two cores: the Pacific Northwest and interior Northwest, where shading reaches the 80-90 percent range, and the southeastern quadrant from Texas through Florida and the Carolinas, where probabilities reach 90-100 percent. A corridor of lighter orange across the central Plains and upper Midwest sits in the 40-50 percent leaning-above range, suggesting weaker model agreement there and the possibility that near-normal outcomes remain competitive. The sole below-normal signal in the lower 48 is confined to northern New England and possibly adjacent upstate New York, with probabilities in the 33-40 percent leaning-below range — a modest signal at best. Hawaii shows a strong 90-100 percent above-normal signal on the Big Island, while Alaska is split, with the south-central coast and Aleutians leaning above normal and western Alaska carrying a below-normal signal in the 40-50 percent range.

The two-lobed warm pattern — one core anchored in the Northwest, another in the Southeast, with a relative minimum in between across the central interior — is geometrically consistent with a persistent ridge-trough-ridge configuration at upper levels, implying the current amplified western ridge and any eastern downstream ridging are expected to hold rather than flatten through the September 18-22 window. That said, the weakened probability shading across the central Plains compared to both flanking warm cores suggests the mid-level pattern may be somewhat transitional or less amplified over the interior, so a complete, locked-in regime is not what the chart demands — only that significant troughing capable of displacing the warm signals does not materialize over most of the country in this period.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary: This 6-10 day 500 mb height and anomaly forecast, valid 18-22 September 2026, shows a deep cutoff low centered over the Canadian Arctic Archipelago with the innermost closed contour near 5,400 dam, surrounded by tightly packed height contours indicating a strongly amplified negative height anomaly there; the blue dashed anomaly contours reach their most negative values (appearing to approach -10 to -15 dam based on contour spacing and labeling) directly over that Arctic center. A broad ridge axis runs roughly from the southwestern United States northward through the western Plains and into western Canada, where positive anomalies on the order of +5 to +10 dam are indicated by the red dashed contours, but the zero-anomaly line (the transition from red to blue dashed contours) appears to cut through roughly the central to east-central portions of the contiguous United States, suggesting the western ridge is present but not dramatically amplified over the lower 48. The absolute height pattern shows a very amplified, meridionally elongated trough dipping from the Arctic deep into central Canada, with the 5,520 dam contour reaching into the upper Midwest, consistent with a significant downstream troughing signal rather than a zonal flow regime. The western ridge does not appear to be strongly building poleward; positive anomalies are confined largely to the western U.S. and western Canada below the trough center, implying the ridge amplitude is modest and not extending aggressively into higher latitudes. Overall the pattern is decidedly amplified and meridional rather than zonal, dominated by the deep Arctic cutoff low and its downstream trough over central and eastern Canada.

sources.title: CPC 8-14 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary: This chart is a 500 mb height and height-anomaly prognostic valid 20–26 September 2026, made 12 September 2026, so it qualifies as the 8–14 day product. The dominant feature is a deep, positively tilted trough centered over the Canadian Arctic Archipelago, with the lowest heights near or just north of Hudson Bay; the height contours close tightly there, suggesting a cutoff-like or strongly amplified cyclonic circulation over the high Arctic. Over western North America the height contours are broadly anticyclonically curved across the Pacific Northwest and western Canada, but the implied ridge axis appears to run north-south near or just west of the Rockies rather than sitting squarely over the northern Rockies or northern Plains — the 576–582 dam contours across the contiguous United States Southwest and central Plains suggest the ridge core has retreated somewhat westward and southward rather than dominating the northern Rockies and northern Plains. The dashed anomaly contours (purple/blue negative over the Arctic, red positive over the mid-latitudes) show a positive anomaly center most clearly expressed over the north-central Pacific and the U.S. interior, with the most prominent negative anomaly confined well north of 60°N over the Arctic; the positive anomaly over western Canada and the northern Rockies appears modest at best, not a strongly amplified positive center in that region. The overall pattern implies a vigorous polar vortex extension toward Hudson Bay, a downstream ridge across the central and southern Rockies, and a downstream trough implied over the eastern U.S. by the height-contour spacing there, though the anomaly magnitudes over western Canada fall short of a classic strongly positive western ridge signal.

sources.title: WPC Short Range Forecast Discussion
sources.summary: A robust upper-trough pushes a well-defined cold front eastward today, with isolated to scattered heavy rainfall and severe weather possible across the Northeast to Central Plains, especially this morning and afternoon. The front exits into the Atlantic by tomorrow, improving Eastern conditions. Meanwhile, a consolidating low pressure system in the Northwest maintains unsettled conditions across the Western and Central U.S., with daily thunderstorm rounds in the Heartland posing enhanced heavy rainfall and flash flood threats. Monsoon storms persist over the Southern Rockies and Four Corners with excessive rainfall risk. Frontal passages bring pleasant 60s-70s temperatures to the Northern Tier and High Plains, while an upper-ridge lingers over the Southern Plains and Mid-Mississippi Valley, threatening record heat into the work week.

sources.title: SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook
sources.summary:
Marginal risk of severe thunderstorms across the Ohio Valley into the Northeast and central/northern High Plains through Monday morning.

Ohio Valley/Northeast: Strong upper trough and westerly mid-level jet will push a cold front eastward this afternoon-evening. Despite marginal instability from weak lapse rates and cloud cover, organized convection expected along/ahead of the front mid-afternoon from Ohio into western New York, spreading quickly eastward. Deep-layer shear (35-45 kt) supports supercells initially, but clusters and bowing segments with isolated damaging wind threat likely develop as convection moves east and weakens with nocturnal cooling.

High Plains: Weak diurnal instability ahead of a closed upper low moving into the northern Rockies. Isolated thunderstorms possible late afternoon across northeast Colorado into southeast Wyoming with marginal severe hail/wind potential. Elevated convection increases late tonight into Monday across western South Dakota toward the Mid-Missouri Valley with isolated hail threat.

Long Island/Southern New England: Ongoing morning bands with embedded storms. Minimal surface-based instability; mostly elevated thunderstorms expected, though low-level shear will be monitored for potential surface-based development.

sources.title: SPC Mesoscale Discussions
sources.summary: No mesoscale discussions currently active. No organized convective threat is being monitored by SPC at this time.

sources.title: NHC Tropical Weather Outlooks
sources.summary:
Atlantic: A trough of low pressure over the central subtropical Atlantic with disorganized convection shows minimal development potential through 48 hours due to strong upper-level winds, but could develop gradually (20 percent chance) by mid-to-late week as it moves into more favorable conditions.

East Pacific: Tropical Storm Norbert is active. A separate low pressure system several hundred miles southwest of Baja California's southern tip is producing disorganized showers and thunderstorms. Development is expected to be favorable, with high probability (80 percent) of tropical depression formation within 48 hours as the system moves westward.

sources.title: ENSO State (Oceanic Niño Index)
sources.summary: Cold ENSO conditions are weakening. The most recent ONI value (NDJ 2025) is -0.60, marking the tail end of La Niña. Forecasts show a transition through neutral conditions by late winter, with warming anomalies developing through spring and summer 2026. By mid-year, anomalies are expected to reach +1.80, indicating onset of El Niño conditions by late summer.

sources.title: Teleconnection Indices (PNA, AO, NAO)
sources.summary: PNA remains modestly negative (-0.34), essentially flat over 14 days around -0.5 to -0.6, offering weak directional support for western ridging and eastern troughing. AO swung from negative (high-latitude blocking tendency) through midperiod to positive (+0.53 latest), with 7-day mean near zero and high daily variability; weak signal overall. NAO has fallen notably into negative territory (-0.66, 7-day mean -1.01 down from -0.51 prior week), suggesting weakened Atlantic ridge-to-trough progression and potential for eastern features to become increasingly negatively tilted or cut off. Summer teleconnection weakness limits direct forecast reliance, but NAO's recent negative trend warrants monitoring.
